item.title: Trump's favorite Democrat threatens to join GOP again — on one condition
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: John Fetterman says he could leave the Democratic Party if Senate Democrats replace Chuck Schumer with Chris Van Hollen, whose criticism of Israel the Pennsylvania senator considers disqualifying. That is the condition behind Fetterman’s latest flirtation with a party switch: not a break over LGBTQ rights, marijuana policy or domestic economics, but a warning that his allegiance may depend on whether his caucus chooses a leader willing to challenge Israel and confront Donald Trump more aggressiv
item.content:encoded:
John Fetterman says he could leave the Democratic Party if Senate Democrats replace Chuck Schumer with Chris Van Hollen, whose criticism of Israel the Pennsylvania senator considers disqualifying. That is the condition behind Fetterman’s latest flirtation with a party switch: not a break over LGBTQ rights, marijuana policy or domestic economics, but a warning that his allegiance may depend on whether his caucus chooses a leader willing to challenge Israel and confront Donald Trump more aggressively.

The ultimatum, delivered Saturday on Fox News, also clarifies what Fetterman’s cultivated political estrangement is doing. He is using the possibility of defection to pressure Democratic senators over their own leadership decision while presenting resistance to Trump as partisan spectacle and opposition to Israeli policy as hostility toward Israel itself.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An ultimatum built around Israel

Asked about the prospect of Van Hollen replacing Schumer, Fetterman said a caucus decision favoring the Maryland senator would be “troubling.”

“Yeah, absolutely,” he said when asked whether it could push him out of the party. Fetterman described Van Hollen as having made his name by being “very … hostile to Israel.”

That wording collapses several distinct positions into one politically useful accusation. According to AlterNet, Van Hollen has gained support from voters who want stronger opposition to the Trump administration and its harshest policies. Fetterman’s objection, however, centered on Israel and on Democratic lawmakers who favor withholding or conditioning assistance.

“Both in the House now and the Senate now, their first instincts are to punish Israel and to withhold these kinds of aid,” Fetterman said, arguing that Iran should instead be held accountable.

Fetterman has been one of the Senate’s staunchest supporters of Israel. Schumer shares that broad alignment, and Fetterman is backing him in the leadership contest. His intervention therefore is not merely an observation about feeling unwelcome among Democrats. It is an attempt to attach a potential institutional cost—his departure—to the caucus’s choice of leader.

“Country over party,” with Trump spared

Fetterman also defended the Trump administration from blame for high gasoline prices, saying that although Americans were suffering, he continued to blame Iran as well. He called his position “a political loser” but framed it as “country over party.”

That slogan does substantial work. It casts Fetterman’s own breaks with Democrats as principled independence while depicting investigations of Trump as partisan retaliation. He urged lawmakers to embrace bipartisanship during the administration’s final two years and warned against turning Congress into “a circus of constant hearings about payback.”

Congressional oversight, however, is not inherently payback. Hearings are among the legislature’s few direct tools for investigating executive conduct. By preemptively describing sustained scrutiny as circus politics, Fetterman adopts a framing that benefits the official whose administration would face examination: Trump. The people demanding accountability become the source of dysfunction; the administration exercising federal power recedes from view.

The same misdirection operates in Fetterman’s discussion of Israel. Lawmakers considering restrictions on aid are exercising authority over American resources and policy. Labeling that position punishment or hostility avoids the underlying dispute: whether unconditional U.S. support should continue and whether Democratic leaders may impose limits without being accused of antagonism toward an allied country.

A Democrat by ballot, an ally by choice

Fetterman entered the Senate after winning election in 2022 as a progressive. Since then, AlterNet reports, he has moved sharply right on several prominent issues, repeatedly broken with his caucus and supported Trump, particularly where U.S. policy toward Israel is concerned.

He has also said he would be an awkward fit in the Republican Party because he continues to support LGBTQ rights and marijuana legalization. Those positions complicate the partisan branding but do not erase the practical effect of his conduct. Party identity is less consequential than how a senator uses power: whom he protects, which policies he enables and what price he tries to impose on colleagues who dissent.

AlterNet reports that fears of a Fetterman defection have become less urgent after Democrats won 56 Senate seats in the midterms. That larger majority reduces his leverage over control of the chamber. His threat can still influence a leadership fight, but it no longer carries the same capacity to throw the majority into immediate chaos.

That may explain the increasingly explicit terms. A vague reputation for independence produces attention; a conditional threat names the demand. Keep Schumer, reject Van Hollen and preserve a leadership posture Fetterman regards as sufficiently supportive of Israel—or risk losing him.

The voters he left behind

Fetterman is expected to face serious Democratic primary opposition when he is next up for election in 2028. AlterNet also reports that his approval among Democratic voters has collapsed, putting a potential reelection bid in jeopardy.

That political weakness matters because Fetterman’s alienation is often narrated as though the party simply drifted away from him. The chronology points in the other direction. He won office as a progressive, changed his posture after securing a six-year term and now invokes leaving the party when its members consider leadership he opposes.

His Fox News appearance turns that record into an ultimatum aimed upward at Senate Democrats and outward at dissatisfied voters: accommodate his priorities or accept his departure. But with Democrats holding 56 seats, the caucus may have less reason to treat one senator’s threatened defection as a veto. The more immediate judgment belongs to Pennsylvania Democrats, who will eventually decide whether the label Fetterman still carries bears any meaningful relationship to the senator he has chosen to become.

item.title: MAGA Americans explain why they’ve turned on ‘clown’ Trump
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A group of Mississippi voters who previously backed Donald Trump told Bulwark publisher Sarah Longwell that they supported Democrat Colom instead of Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, citing Trump’s conduct, his family’s business ties and Hyde-Smith’s loyalty to him. Their revolt does not establish a national realignment. item.content:encoded:
A group of Mississippi voters who previously backed Donald Trump told Bulwark publisher Sarah Longwell that they supported Democrat Colom instead of Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, citing Trump’s conduct, his family’s business ties and Hyde-Smith’s loyalty to him. Their revolt does not establish a national realignment. It does show something more specific: for these voters, Trump’s endorsement had become a liability, and a Democratic vote offered the most immediate way to restrain a president they once helped empower.

The headline shorthand—that “MAGA Americans” have turned on Trump—claims more than focus-group interviews can demonstrate. These are disaffected Trump voters in deep-red Mississippi, not the whole of his movement. But their explanations matter because they attack the premise on which Trump has built his political authority: that personal loyalty to him is both the measure of Republican legitimacy and proof of opposition to a corrupt establishment.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Hyde-Smith made Trump the choice

One participant told Longwell that Hyde-Smith’s billboards showing her embracing Trump were the “main reason” she voted for Colom. Her opinion of the president had deteriorated to a blunt verdict: “He’s a clown.”

The voter also accused Hyde-Smith of enriching herself and acting in her own interest, then expressed hope that Colom would be different. Another white woman, who described herself as a strong Republican and said she had previously voted for Hyde-Smith, rejected her this time because she regarded the Republican as “Trump’s yes-person.”

That is the political cost of turning a party into a personal loyalty system. Hyde-Smith’s advertised proximity to the president was meant to transfer his authority to her campaign. For these voters, it transferred their distrust instead. They were not confused about whom the imagery represented or what it demanded: a vote for Hyde-Smith was presented as a vote for Trump, so they voted for her opponent.

The corruption story reached Trump’s family

The participants’ complaints extended beyond Trump’s temperament. One former supporter pointed to Trump family connections with prediction-market companies Kalshi and Polymarket, noting Donald Trump Jr.’s reported service on Polymarket’s advisory board, and called the arrangement “very, very self-serving.”

Another voter described Trump as a “full-fledged narcissist” and said she believed his inability to seek another presidential term had left him free to do “whatever he wants to do.” She added that it appeared he was making substantial money from the presidency and raised concerns about spending controversies involving members of his family, including Jared Kushner and Donald Trump Jr.

Those comments are the voters’ assessments, not findings established by the focus groups. Their political significance lies in where responsibility landed. Trump has long prospered by portraying corruption as something done by distant officials, hostile bureaucrats and entrenched elites. These former supporters now see the White House and the president’s relatives as part of the machinery they distrust.

The shift is not necessarily ideological. One Colom voter still professed affection for Marco Rubio, Jim Jordan and Harold Ford Jr. Her complaint was that Washington corruption was pervasive and that officeholders often succumbed to it. The Democratic vote was therefore less an embrace of a new political program than an attempt to impose a check on the Republican leader.

A vote for restraint, not absolution

“I do hope that with the Democrats taking over, that means they’ll keep him in check better,” one woman told Longwell. That sentence identifies the institutional calculation more clearly than the insults do. Trump holds the presidency; Republican candidates who define themselves through obedience help consolidate his power; electing Democrats is one available mechanism for limiting it.

Another former Trump voter dispensed with any suggestion that his character had only recently become visible. “We all know who he is at this point,” she said. “And we all supported him for a while. We’ve seen this show.”

That admission narrows the excuse. These voters are not describing a politician who concealed every relevant trait until after winning their support. They are describing a bargain they once accepted and now find intolerable, particularly when personal rule, family advantage and party submission appear together.

Longwell’s interviews cannot tell us how widely that judgment extends, and AlterNet’s sweeping MAGA framing outruns the evidence presented. But the Mississippi accounts capture a concrete failure in Trump’s patronage politics: candidates who make loyalty to him their chief credential also inherit the backlash when former supporters decide the loyalty itself is the problem.

item.title: Ex-Trump official takes savage swipe at successor after chaotic meltdown
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Kristi Noem’s “savage swipe” at her successor amounted to a cryptic social-media post, not an explanation of the nationwide airport ground stop that stranded and confused travelers for hours on Friday. The substantive failure belonged to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who could neither give the public a consistent account of the telecommunications outage nor agree on whether new government equipment contributed to it. That distinction matter
item.content:encoded:
Kristi Noem’s “savage swipe” at her successor amounted to a cryptic social-media post, not an explanation of the nationwide airport ground stop that stranded and confused travelers for hours on Friday. The substantive failure belonged to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who could neither give the public a consistent account of the telecommunications outage nor agree on whether new government equipment contributed to it.

That distinction matters. Noem’s mockery supplied the spectacle, but Mullin and Duffy controlled the agencies responsible for explaining a major disruption to national air travel. Their contradictory answers turned an operational breakdown into a crisis of government credibility.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Two officials, two versions of the failure

At their news conference, Mullin suggested that technology installed under Duffy was producing communication errors by “overwhelming the older system.” Duffy disputed that account, saying, “all of the new equipment that we put in, none of that went down.”

Those statements do not resolve whether newer equipment indirectly burdened an older system; they expose a basic disagreement between the officials presenting the government’s response. Travelers were left with a vague reference to a telecommunications outage and no coherent account of how it produced a nationwide, multi-hour halt.

Mullin compounded the confusion when asked whether a cyberattack had caused the incident. He first declared that “there is actually no cyber attack,” then retreated to “there’s nothing completely certain right now.” The responsible answer, if the investigation remained incomplete, was to say exactly that. Instead, Mullin offered certainty and uncertainty in the same appearance.

The problem was not merely poor presentation. Officials speaking before the cause was settled blurred the line between what the government knew and what it wanted the public to believe it knew. Duffy’s rebuttal also shifted attention toward protecting his equipment record while the central question—why the system failed badly enough to stop travel nationwide—remained unanswered.

Noem’s rebuke carries its own baggage

Noem responded on X that she had been “looking for something encouraging to post about that press conference, the security of our nation, the honesty of our press,” before turning to prayer: “Please dear Jesus, bless America and keep us in your hands.” She attached a photograph of her granddaughter Addie.

The post plainly conveyed contempt for the performance without identifying a factual error or offering information about the outage. It was political needling dressed as lamentation: evocative enough to circulate, empty enough to avoid accountability for a specific claim.

Noem is also an awkward messenger for administrative competence. Trump fired her as homeland security secretary in March 2026 after mounting controversies, scrutiny of her leadership and pressure from lawmakers. She faced criticism on Capitol Hill over a $220 million taxpayer-funded DHS advertising campaign featuring her at Mount Rushmore, as well as questions involving transparency, conflicts of interest and her use of a luxury jet. Her tenure also encompassed the fallout from fatal shootings in Minneapolis during aggressive federal immigration operations.

After her removal, the administration placed her in a newly created position as special envoy for the Shield of the Americas, a Western Hemisphere security initiative. She defended her record, while TIME senior correspondent Phillip Ellicott assessed that her dismissal was driven more by optics than by a substantive break with the administration. Ellicott wrote that her personal life, living arrangements, collapsing morale and leadership feuds had made a former Trump favorite “a liability.”

Noem’s criticism therefore should not be mistaken for institutional accountability. It is an ousted official exploiting her successors’ visible failure after surviving her own controversies with another government title.

The spectacle protects the people in charge

AlterNet’s framing centers the personal insult: the former secretary landing a “savage swipe” after a “chaotic meltdown.” That captures the social-media drama but risks misdirecting attention from the officials with present authority.

Noem’s post did not ground aircraft. Travelers did not need her blessing, her granddaughter’s photograph or another round of intra-administration score-settling. They needed Mullin and Duffy to establish what failed, distinguish confirmed facts from unresolved possibilities and explain how the government would prevent another shutdown.

Instead, the public received competing technical stories, an unsupported burst of certainty about a cyberattack and an immediate retreat from that certainty. Noem recognized an opening and took it. Her opportunism is revealing, but the governing failure remains with the officials who stood before the country and demonstrated that they were not yet capable of giving one reliable account of what their own systems had done.

item.title: Security expert torches Trump official for ‘perhaps the worst’ presser ever
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Richard Clarke, a former counterterrorism official who served several presidential administrations, called Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s response to a nationwide FAA ground stop “perhaps the worst crisis communications press conference” he had seen. His criticism was not merely about presentation. After a disruption reportedly stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers, Trump administration officials offered an explanation while, in Clarke’s assessment, lacking the analysis needed to ru
item.content:encoded:
Richard Clarke, a former counterterrorism official who served several presidential administrations, called Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s response to a nationwide FAA ground stop “perhaps the worst crisis communications press conference” he had seen. His criticism was not merely about presentation. After a disruption reportedly stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers, Trump administration officials offered an explanation while, in Clarke’s assessment, lacking the analysis needed to rule out a cyberattack.

Duffy said at a Friday-night White House news conference that a router became overloaded during a routine telecommunications upgrade, producing a multi-hour halt in air travel. But AlterNet reported that remarks by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appeared to conflict with Duffy’s account. Instead of establishing a clear chain of events, the administration’s public response left basic questions about the failure—and the confidence behind its claims—unresolved.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Certainty before analysis

Clarke told CNN host Michael Smerconish that officials should not exclude a cyber cause before completing forensic and root-cause analyses.

“First of all, you should never rule out cyber until you’ve done a forensic analysis or root cause analysis, and they haven’t had time to do that,” Clarke said. Announcing that an incident was not cyber-related while simultaneously acknowledging uncertainty, he argued, was premature.

That distinction matters. Duffy controls the Transportation Department’s public response, but his office’s authority does not make an early technical explanation conclusive. When a system with nationwide consequences fails, political officials can disclose what investigators know, identify what remains under review and avoid claiming more certainty than the evidence supports. According to Clarke, Duffy and Mullin instead delivered a muddled combination: a proposed cause, an unexplained overload and a confident dismissal of another possibility.

Clarke allowed that Duffy’s account might prove correct. But he questioned why a router would become overloaded on an otherwise unremarkable Friday afternoon and argued that the public needed a fuller explanation. The problem was not that officials lacked an immediate final answer. It was that they appeared to get ahead of the investigation while failing to explain the basis for doing so.

A system failure became a leadership failure

Clarke has worked across Republican and Democratic administrations, including those of Ronald Reagan, George H.W. Bush and Barack Obama. He compared the White House appearance unfavorably even with press conferences led by county sheriffs during active-shooter emergencies.

“That press conference yesterday with Duffy and Mullin did not inspire confidence,” he said.

The administration’s performance shifted attention from the operational breakdown to the credibility of the people describing it. Hundreds of thousands of stranded travelers needed to know what had failed, whether the system was secure and what officials were doing to prevent another shutdown. Duffy’s account, as reported, supplied a label—router overload—without satisfying Clarke that the government understood the underlying cause.

That is a consequential failure of public authority. Crisis communication is not cosmetic work performed after the real decisions. It is part of the government’s responsibility during a nationwide disruption, particularly when officials are asking the public to accept technical assurances that ordinary travelers cannot independently test.

Politicians cannot investigate themselves into credibility

Clarke proposed creating a strong cyber equivalent of the National Transportation Safety Board: an expert institution capable of entering major incidents, determining what happened and reporting its findings independently of the politicians managing the fallout.

“We need a voice that we can trust,” he said. “We need experts looking at this thing.”

His proposal identifies the institutional weakness exposed by the ground stop. The government’s immediate account came from political appointees whose incentives include containing panic and defending their administration’s competence. Those incentives do not prove that Duffy’s explanation was false, but they make transparent, expert investigation essential—especially when officials appear to disagree and the technical work is unfinished.

The disruption also followed a Microsoft system shutdown that, according to AlterNet, left millions of people, including government employees, without email access. That timing did not establish that the FAA failure was a cyberattack, and Clarke did not claim that it did. His point was narrower and more defensible: coincidence remains possible, but so does hostile action, and government officials should not erase one possibility before specialists have done the work.

Duffy may ultimately be vindicated on the router explanation. But his Friday-night performance asked Americans to trust a conclusion that Clarke said the administration was not yet equipped to make. In a crisis affecting the national transportation system, reassurance without demonstrated knowledge is not competence. It is a substitute for it.

item.title: Trump has retreated to his 'bunker' as nation turns on him: leaker
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s response to a punishing midterm defeat has not been retreat from power so much as retreat into loyalty. As AlterNet recounts from Guardian reporting, the president has surrounded himself with increasingly compliant advisers while congressional Republicans continue protecting him from accountability. The “bunker” is figurative: former Homeland Security official Miles Taylor used the term to describe an isolated leader relying on aides willing to indulge his most extreme demands, no
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s response to a punishing midterm defeat has not been retreat from power so much as retreat into loyalty. As AlterNet recounts from Guardian reporting, the president has surrounded himself with increasingly compliant advisers while congressional Republicans continue protecting him from accountability. The “bunker” is figurative: former Homeland Security official Miles Taylor used the term to describe an isolated leader relying on aides willing to indulge his most extreme demands, not a president physically hiding from public view.

Democrats won the national midterm vote by 13 percentage points and captured Republican strongholds in Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas. The Guardian attributed the backlash to an eight-month war in Iran, surging fuel prices and tariffs that drove up living costs. Yet Republicans have shown little appetite for confronting the president whose policies the reporting identifies as central to their defeat.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Electoral rejection without a Republican revolt

Trump’s conduct after the losses has alternated between attempted conciliation, aggression and spectacle. One episode captured the disorder: he offered White House press secretary to UFC chief Dana White, then described the invitation as a joke. Whether that appointment was floated accidentally or impulsively, the reversal suggested an administration in which personnel decisions can become presidential improvisation.

The more consequential response is taking shape beyond the farce. Taylor, who served during Trump’s first administration and later became a whistleblower, told the Guardian that Trump was ending up with “the bottom of the barrel appointees”—officials selected less for independent judgment than for their willingness to conform.

“Like any wannabe autocrat, you end up in the figurative bunker at the end of the regime with the most hardcore loyalists,” Taylor said. His warning concerns the machinery of government, not Trump’s mood. A politically weakened president retains command of the executive branch, substantial authority over foreign policy and a party still unwilling to impose meaningful restraint.

Stephen Miller and the strategy of crossing the line

Taylor identified Trump’s new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, as an example of the danger posed by an administration that treats legal limits as obstacles to test. Recalling their service together during Trump’s first term, Taylor said Miller was willing to approach the boundary of the law, cross it and force courts to intervene.

That account describes a governing strategy: act first, transfer the burden of resistance to judges and exploit the time between an unlawful order and its enforcement. Taylor said he fears Trump could eventually defy judicial rulings, including an order from the Supreme Court, if aides provide him with arguments for doing so.

The report does not establish that Trump has decided to take that step. It does establish why Taylor considers it plausible: Trump now has a team that may be more willing to rationalize escalation than to prevent it. The distinction matters. Institutional breakdown rarely begins with a formal announcement that legal authority no longer counts. It begins when officials calculate that compliance with the leader is safer than compliance with the law.

Congress chooses protection over correction

Republican lawmakers had an opportunity to respond to historic losses by reassessing the president’s leadership. Instead, according to the Guardian, the party helped kill an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and elected Trump ally Jim Jordan as House minority leader for the next Congress.

Those decisions make the power structure plain. Trump may have suffered a major electoral repudiation, but Republican officeholders remain unwilling to translate that result into institutional resistance. Their behavior insulates him from the political consequences voters imposed on the party and leaves the executive branch’s internal loyalists as an even more important source of advice and control.

Calling this merely Trump’s “bunker” risks making the problem sound psychological: a defeated man sulking among flatterers. The sharper fact is that congressional Republicans are helping construct the shelter. Isolation at the top becomes dangerous when the president’s party continues supplying protection from outside.

Foreign policy with fewer restraints

Taylor also pointed to foreign policy, where presidential authority is broad and the consequences of impulsive action can be immediate. After the war in Iran reported by the Guardian, he raised two questions about the remaining years of Trump’s term: whether NATO would survive and whether the United States might attempt to seize additional territory.

Trump has discussed such actions before, Taylor said, but advisers pulled him back during his first two terms. Taylor is no longer confident that the current circle will do the same. That is a warning, not a report that either decision has been made. But the personnel shift changes the risk: advisers who once constrained presidential impulses are being replaced by people chosen for loyalty or ideological alignment.

The country turned sharply against Trump’s party at the ballot box, according to the reported results. The Republican establishment’s answer was not to restrain the president whose policies helped produce that judgment. It preserved his protection in Congress, elevated another loyalist and left him governing through an increasingly deferential inner circle. Trump lost political support; he did not lose the powers of the presidency.

item.title: A major pillar of the GOP base just imploded — and no one saw it coming
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Republican Party’s white evangelical turnout machine faltered in the November midterms, but calling that result an “implosion” outruns the evidence. An American Communities Project analysis reported by The Washington Post found sharply reduced participation and weaker Republican voting across 343 heavily evangelical counties in 15 states with Senate races. That is a serious breach in a coalition the GOP has relied on for decades. It is not yet proof that the coalition has collapsed. The dist
item.content:encoded:
The Republican Party’s white evangelical turnout machine faltered in the November midterms, but calling that result an “implosion” outruns the evidence. An American Communities Project analysis reported by The Washington Post found sharply reduced participation and weaker Republican voting across 343 heavily evangelical counties in 15 states with Senate races. That is a serious breach in a coalition the GOP has relied on for decades. It is not yet proof that the coalition has collapsed.

The distinction matters because electoral power is measured in votes delivered repeatedly, not in dramatic post-election metaphors. These counties produced only 66 percent as many votes as they did in the 2024 presidential election. Surrounding counties in the same states reached 78 percent of their 2024 totals. According to ACP founder Dante Chinni, matching neighboring turnout rates could have supplied Republicans with hundreds of thousands of additional votes.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The missing votes came from Republican strongholds

ACP classifies the places it examined as “evangelical hub counties,” meaning they contain unusually high concentrations of people who identify as evangelical, particularly white evangelicals. Nearly all are in the Southeast, stretching from Texas to Virginia.

White evangelicals make up 52 percent of the population in those counties, compared with 13 percent nationwide, according to the Public Religion Research Institute’s 2023 Census of American Religion. These are not marginal constituencies or culturally mixed swing districts. They are communities situated inside one of the Republican Party’s most dependable sources of electoral power.

Their reduced participation therefore carried an asymmetrical cost. Chinni told the Post that enthusiasm in the evangelical hubs was lower than in other places. Because these counties normally vote heavily Republican, every missing voter was more damaging to the GOP than an equivalent turnout decline in politically balanced territory.

Researchers and pollsters were still examining the election results, according to the reporting, so the county analysis cannot by itself establish why participation fell. It does show where the Republican machine failed to produce its customary volume.

Trump’s transaction with evangelical voters is showing strain

Paul Binford, a 69-year-old Kentucky evangelical and regular Republican voter, offered one explanation for withdrawing support. He and his wife concluded that President Donald Trump was preoccupied with “enriching himself” rather than governing effectively.

“We thought he might not sell us out, but he was [the] worst offender of all,” Binford said.

One voter’s account cannot explain hundreds of counties. It does, however, expose the vulnerability in a political arrangement often presented as an alliance of shared conviction. Republican leaders received votes, institutional protection and moral cover from white evangelical communities. In exchange, those voters expected political power to serve their priorities. Binford’s complaint is not that Trump violated a standard imposed by his opponents; it is that he failed the bargain his own supporters believed they had made.

That is more politically consequential than a sudden change in theological doctrine. The available evidence points to demobilization and diminished Republican loyalty, not to a wholesale ideological realignment. Voters can stay home because they feel used without becoming Democrats. A weakened transaction is not the same thing as a transformed electorate.

A history too durable for one election to erase

The modern Christian right was built through institutions, not merely enthusiasm. Jerry Falwell Sr., the Liberty University founder and Moral Majority co-founder, helped turn conservative white evangelical identity into organized Republican power beginning in the late 1970s and 1980s.

That project carried the politics of the segregated South into a new partisan structure. Falwell had attacked Martin Luther King Jr. and defended segregation, declaring that “the true Negro does not want integration.” His later national prominence did not erase that record. The Christian right’s rise also overlapped with the Republican Southern Strategy, through which the party attracted white conservative voters alienated by civil rights and the Democratic Party’s changing direction.

But the supplied results do not establish that “even racism” failed to mobilize evangelical voters this year. That framing substitutes an asserted motive for an observed electoral result. The analysis measured turnout and Republican performance; it did not demonstrate that racial appeals were attempted, rejected or decisive. The history is relevant because it explains how this voting bloc was assembled and whom its politics often served. It does not relieve reporters of the obligation to distinguish that history from what the new data can prove.

A warning for the GOP, not an obituary

Republicans still hold the institutional advantages created by decades of evangelical organizing: churches, political networks, conservative media, donor relationships and communities accustomed to treating GOP participation as a cultural duty. One midterm turnout collapse does not make those structures disappear.

What it does reveal is that party leaders cannot treat those voters as an automatic resource. The reported deficit was large enough to matter, concentrated enough to identify and rooted in counties Republicans normally expect to carry their candidates. If disillusionment with Trump contributed to the decline, the party faces a problem of its own making: it concentrated authority and attention around a leader whose conduct at least some loyal evangelical voters now describe as self-serving.

The Republican evangelical pillar did not demonstrably implode. It failed under load. Whether that failure becomes a lasting fracture will depend on whether voters such as the Binfords return—and whether Republican leaders can persuade them that the transaction has anything left to offer besides another demand for obedience.

item.title: Trump just admitted his failure in one stunning move
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump has reassigned Vice President JD Vance after Republicans’ historic losses in the 2026 midterms, a move Rohit Kachroo of the i Paper interprets as Trump’s closest approximation to admitting that the war with Iran has failed politically as well as strategically. Vance had blamed the Republican defeat on the war’s fallout. By demoting him, Trump has acted on that diagnosis without publicly accepting responsibility for the policy that produced it. The distinction matters. Vance did not
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump has reassigned Vice President JD Vance after Republicans’ historic losses in the 2026 midterms, a move Rohit Kachroo of the i Paper interprets as Trump’s closest approximation to admitting that the war with Iran has failed politically as well as strategically. Vance had blamed the Republican defeat on the war’s fallout. By demoting him, Trump has acted on that diagnosis without publicly accepting responsibility for the policy that produced it.

The distinction matters. Vance did not launch the war, and voters did not give him presidential authority over it. Trump holds that power. Reassigning a subordinate allows the president to acknowledge electoral damage while directing attention toward the messenger—and away from the decision-maker.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A demotion in place of an admission

Kachroo reports that Vance’s reassignment was also driven by his failure to meet expectations in the vice-presidential role. But its timing, after Vance connected Republican losses to the Iran conflict and polling reportedly reflected similar voter concerns, gives the move an unmistakable political function.

Trump is changing personnel as the costs of his policy become harder to deny. Nearly a year into the conflict, according to the account, the United States, Israel and Iran have all failed to achieve their ultimate objectives. Republicans have lost control by historic margins. Israel has absorbed further economic damage, while its elections have opened a possible route for the opposition bloc to remove Benjamin Netanyahu and end what critics call his “October 7 government.”

Those outcomes do not turn Vance into an innocent bystander; he served in the administration carrying out the policy. But the hierarchy is not ambiguous. Trump made the consequential choice. Vance became expendable when the consequences reached the ballot box.

Trump’s rhetoric keeps undercutting his retreat

Even as Trump reportedly attempts to change course, his public claims continue to obstruct that effort. “We’ve got their Strait,” he recently declared, referring to the Strait of Hormuz. Kachroo argues that the assertion is false. Oil prices surged again after Trump suggested that reaching a deal with Iran was no longer necessary.

That is not merely careless messaging around a distant conflict. Control of the strait bears directly on energy markets, and presidential declarations can impose immediate economic costs. Trump’s posture asks the public to see domination where the reported conditions show instability—and to absorb higher prices as the cost of maintaining the image.

Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, offered a sharply different assessment, saying the strait would “never return” to its prewar condition. His statement is Iran’s position, not a settled forecast. But it underscores the danger Trump’s boasts evade: the conflict may be hardening into a prolonged state of confrontation that no participant can quickly reverse.

The war strengthened what it was meant to weaken

Kachroo writes that Iran’s retaliation has revealed both the country’s reach and its limitations. That combination helps explain why military pressure has not produced a clean strategic victory. Iran has suffered, but it has retained enough capacity to impose continuing costs. Israel has suffered economically and politically. The United States has suffered electoral and energy-price consequences.

The most damning result is that the war may have fortified some of the leaders and political forces Washington intended to weaken. Military action can expose an adversary’s vulnerabilities while simultaneously giving that adversary new grounds for mobilization, retaliation and domestic legitimacy. A campaign sold through the language of control can instead create a durable system of mutual coercion.

With a substantially changed Congress taking office in the new year, Trump may face institutional constraints that electoral defeat alone could not impose. His reassignment of Vance suggests he recognizes the political emergency. His continued triumphalism suggests he still wants recognition without accountability: a course correction presented as command, and a presidential failure deposited on the vice president’s desk.

item.title: Psychologist exposes 'the strangest speech' Trump has given in a long time
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: AlterNet’s headline promises an exposure. What its report actually provides is narrower: clinical and forensic psychologist John Paul Garrison watched clips from President Donald Trump’s Wednesday Veterans Day speech and argued in a Friday YouTube video that Trump appeared unable to read, improvise, or speak clearly. item.content:encoded:
AlterNet’s headline promises an exposure. What its report actually provides is narrower: clinical and forensic psychologist John Paul Garrison watched clips from President Donald Trump’s Wednesday Veterans Day speech and argued in a Friday YouTube video that Trump appeared unable to read, improvise, or speak clearly. Garrison called it Trump’s strangest speech in some time and suggested the performance could help explain what he described as the president’s reduced participation in informal press appearances after the midterms.

The speech may warrant scrutiny. The diagnosis remains Garrison’s interpretation, not an established medical finding.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A halting performance becomes a remote diagnosis

According to AlterNet, Trump stumbled almost immediately and had particular difficulty whenever he departed from his teleprompter. Garrison said the president struggled to articulate words and sometimes appeared not to understand the prepared text.

The psychologist highlighted several passages. Trump referred to the “jungles” of Afghanistan while recounting a soldier’s service, called the Taliban an “evil group,” followed that with the fragment “terrorists all,” and had trouble pronouncing “eardrums.” Garrison interpreted the remarks as disconnected verbal fragments rather than ordinary misstatements.

“What you’re seeing is that he’s just saying whatever random fragments of words come to his mind,” Garrison said. He later suggested that Trump’s difficulty speaking could reflect “some sort of event” interfering with his speech.

That interpretation is serious, but AlterNet’s reporting does not establish it as a diagnosis. Garrison did not examine Trump for the analysis described here; he assessed recorded public behavior. His broader suggestion that Trump may have experienced a stroke is therefore speculation, however firmly he presents it. A specialist’s credentials do not turn video commentary into a neurological examination.

The report weakens its case further by noting Trump’s lack of his usual “glowing orange makeup,” which Garrison called “highly unusual.” A change in cosmetics may be visually conspicuous. On the facts presented, it is not meaningful evidence of neurological impairment.

The relevant institution is the presidency

Trump’s health is not merely personal because he holds presidential power. If a president repeatedly cannot comprehend prepared material, communicate coherently without a script, or participate in unscripted questioning, that has consequences for governance and public accountability. The proper response, however, is documented scrutiny—not diagnosis by montage.

Garrison said Trump appeared to be doing fewer press gaggles after the midterms and favoring prerecorded interviews. AlterNet reports that observation as something he could determine, not as a confirmed change ordered by the White House or supported by a stated schedule comparison. Nor does the account establish why any reduction occurred. The speech may suggest a possible explanation; it does not prove one.

Still, the distinction between live questioning and prerecorded appearances matters. A teleprompter can stabilize a speech. Editing and controlled interview conditions can conceal confusion, remove prolonged mistakes, and limit follow-up questions. If presidential aides are increasingly steering Trump toward those formats, they possess the schedules, access controls, and institutional authority to do it. That would make their conduct part of the story—not because the report proves a concealment effort, but because gatekeeping determines what the public can observe.

Sensational framing obscures the unanswered questions

Calling the remarks “the strangest speech” supplies an irresistible clip-driven hook. It does less to clarify whether Trump’s public performance has changed, whether any change is sustained, and whether the White House has restricted unscripted access in response.

Those are questions about presidential capacity and institutional transparency. They cannot be settled by a YouTube psychologist declaring that a verbal stumble “seemed” to reflect an unspecified neurological event. Nor should they be displaced by chatter about makeup.

The report supports a concrete, limited conclusion: Trump delivered a Veterans Day speech containing halting delivery, verbal difficulty, and several peculiar phrases, and Garrison interpreted those moments as signs of serious neurological decline. It does not establish that Trump suffered a stroke, that his appearance schedule changed because of his health, or that aides deliberately hid a condition.

If Trump’s handlers are replacing open questioning with controlled recordings, the revealing evidence will be in the pattern of access and the decisions behind it. The president’s “orange makeup” is a distraction from that exercise of power.

item.title: Roy Cohn’s Golden Rule led Trump straight into a calamity
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Roy Cohn’s rule was simple: never concede error, never retreat, and never let contrary evidence alter the performance of certainty. New Republic Editor-in-Chief Win McCormack argues that Donald Trump carried that doctrine into his second presidency—and into a series of self-inflicted failures, from tariffs to war with Iran. The calamity, in McCormack’s account, is not merely that Trump made grave mistakes. It is that he built an administration less capable of stopping him from repeating them. Th
item.content:encoded:
Roy Cohn’s rule was simple: never concede error, never retreat, and never let contrary evidence alter the performance of certainty. New Republic Editor-in-Chief Win McCormack argues that Donald Trump carried that doctrine into his second presidency—and into a series of self-inflicted failures, from tariffs to war with Iran. The calamity, in McCormack’s account, is not merely that Trump made grave mistakes. It is that he built an administration less capable of stopping him from repeating them.

That is a consequential argument, but AlterNet’s framing outruns the evidence it presents. The article declares a collapse of Trump’s power while offering McCormack’s interpretation, references to unspecified midterm results, and a psychological account of Trump’s upbringing. What it establishes more clearly is a governing structure organized around presidential impulse and the suppression of internal dissent.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Cohn’s doctrine becomes a staffing policy

McCormack traces Trump’s refusal to yield partly to his childhood. He cites Trump’s niece, Mary L. Trump, who has described her father’s brother as the product of a “cold, ruthless, mercenary father” and a frequently absent, ill mother. McCormack then places Roy Cohn—the ruthless lawyer who served as chief counsel to Sen. Joseph McCarthy—in the role of political tutor.

The lesson McCormack attributes to Cohn was not persistence in pursuit of a sound objective. It was allegiance to a position after reality had discredited it: never bend, regardless of how wrong the claim becomes.

Biographical interpretation cannot substitute for reporting on presidential decisions. The politically relevant part is not whether childhood deprivation explains Trump’s conduct. It is that, according to McCormack, Trump translated an aversion to contradiction into an institutional design. After reportedly bristling at advisers such as retired Marine Gen. John Kelly, Trump filled his second-term Cabinet with people McCormack characterizes as compliant and mediocre—officials unlikely to challenge even his most erratic inclinations.

That choice belongs to Trump. Advisers can fail to resist, but the president selects them, assigns their authority and decides whether unwelcome facts reach the room. A Cabinet constructed for obedience turns personal error into government policy.

Tariffs reward the refusal to learn

McCormack uses tariffs as an example of the cost. Trump, he says, remains committed to the false idea that foreign exporters pay them, despite the burden falling on American importers and ultimately reaching US businesses and consumers through higher costs.

The distinction matters because Trump’s account misdirects responsibility. A tariff imposed by Washington is not a bill that the exporting country simply pays. Presenting it that way lets the president market a domestic tax burden as punishment inflicted abroad.

Under Cohn’s rule, correction itself becomes evidence of disloyalty. Expertise is treated not as a constraint on presidential error but as an obstacle to the story the president wants to tell. Officials chosen for pliancy have every incentive to preserve the fiction and little power—or appetite—to force a reckoning with its consequences.

Military escalation without a corrective mechanism

McCormack extends the same diagnosis to Trump’s attack on Iran. In his account, Trump drew confidence from the successful seizure of Venezuela’s president and imagined that Iran—a country McCormack describes as having an estimated 93.4 million people, roughly 610,000 military personnel and the Revolutionary Guard—could also be subdued.

The reported result was not submission. McCormack says the US attack killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei along with more moderate Iranian leaders whom US analysts believed might have negotiated over Iran’s nuclear program.

Those claims carry enormous weight and, in the supplied account, come through McCormack. They should be treated accordingly. But the political mechanism he identifies is clear: success in one coercive operation became a rationale for attempting a far more dangerous one, while the administration’s internal structure reduced the likelihood of effective opposition.

This is where the Cohn method stops being a personality trait and becomes a national hazard. A president who cannot admit error can impose costs far beyond his own reputation. When advisers are selected for submission, there is no dependable institutional brake between a leader’s analogy and military force.

“Collapse” does not mean the machinery stops

McCormack points to midterm election results as evidence that Trump’s approach ended in political calamity. Yet the AlterNet account supplies no details about those results, and McCormack’s forecast that Trump may spend much of the remainder of his term attending to construction projects is speculation, not a demonstrated transfer of power.

More importantly, political damage does not neutralize presidential authority. McCormack himself warns that Trump could still pursue what he describes as a central project: reversing the country’s demographic transformation through attacks on affirmative-action programs and accelerated deportations of noncitizen residents of color. He suggests those efforts could intensify if Stephen Miller becomes chief of staff.

McCormack interprets that agenda as an attempt to restore an overwhelmingly white United States. The policies he identifies are concrete even where the judgment about Trump’s ultimate objective remains McCormack’s: dismantling affirmative-action programs and expanding rapid deportation. Those actions would be carried out not by Trump’s will alone, but by executive agencies, political appointees and officials willing to convert that will into administrative force.

McCormack closes by predicting that Trump will fail in a broader effort to drag American excellence down to his own level. That flourish is less useful than the institutional warning underneath it. Failure at elections, economics or foreign policy does not necessarily make a president harmless. It can leave an aggrieved officeholder with substantial legal power, fewer internal restraints and an administration trained to treat contradiction as betrayal.

item.title: The day fear lost —and what Trump never saw coming
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: AlterNet’s account of the 2026 midterms presents the Democratic sweep as more than a partisan defeat for Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The voters targeted by MAGA campaigns built around racial resentment, misogyny, nativism and anti-trans panic repeatedly refused the assigned role. The fear did not disappear. It was funded, broadcast and placed on ballots—and, in the contests AlterNet describes, it lost. What Trump and his movement failed to anticipate was not merely Democratic tur
item.content:encoded:
AlterNet’s account of the 2026 midterms presents the Democratic sweep as more than a partisan defeat for Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The voters targeted by MAGA campaigns built around racial resentment, misogyny, nativism and anti-trans panic repeatedly refused the assigned role. The fear did not disappear. It was funded, broadcast and placed on ballots—and, in the contests AlterNet describes, it lost.

What Trump and his movement failed to anticipate was not merely Democratic turnout. It was a transfer of political power toward precisely the people MAGA propaganda had marked as suspect, inferior or dangerous: women, racial minorities, LGBTQ candidates, scientists and union workers. The attempted backlash became the setting for a rejection of the social hierarchy it was designed to protect.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The candidates cast as threats became officeholders

The clearest rebuke came from races in which identity itself had been turned into a Republican campaign weapon.

In Alabama, a Democratic software engineer became the first transgender woman elected to the state legislature, according to AlterNet. She flipped a state House seat despite a campaign that attacked her over her gender. Arizona elected its first Native American woman to statewide office. Nevada and Wisconsin each chose their first Black governor.

Georgia’s results concentrated several historic breakthroughs in one state. Voters elected their first Black woman governor, reelected their first Jewish senator and sent Emory University microbiologist Jasmine Clark to Congress. AlterNet identifies Clark as the first Black woman with a science doctorate elected to the House.

These victories matter because the candidates did not merely survive abstract “polarization.” They prevailed against a political project that made exclusion central to its appeal. Describing that result only as blue defeating red would erase the choice Republican strategists made: to spend heavily on messages intended to turn difference into danger.

The machinery of resentment met its limit

MAGA politics has long treated fear as a renewable electoral resource. Trump’s rise fused white grievance, hostility toward immigrants, contempt for women and theatrical religiosity into a coalition organized as much around cultural domination as conventional policy.

That strategy depends on political misdirection. Economic and institutional power remains concentrated among officeholders, donors and party organizations, but campaign anger is pushed downward—toward immigrants, transgender people, racial minorities and anyone else who can be portrayed as an intruder. Weaker groups become the alleged source of social disorder while the people writing laws and financing propaganda escape scrutiny.

AlterNet reports that Republicans poured millions of dollars into openly hateful advertising during the midterms. Yet the messages proved less effective than anticipated, including among white and male voters whom such campaigns typically sought to mobilize. That does not mean prejudice vanished. It means the Republican apparatus failed, in these races, to convert prejudice into enough votes to preserve power.

The distinction matters. Fear did not simply “lose” in some spontaneous national awakening. Candidates, organizers and voters defeated campaigns whose sponsors had money, party infrastructure and access to the presidency’s political megaphone.

A defeat, not an extinction

Roger Stone, a longtime Trump adviser, once summarized his political method with the claim that “hate is a stronger motivator than love.” The midterm results described by AlterNet exposed the limit of that proposition. Hate can command attention and enforce loyalty, but it is not invincible—and repeating it more loudly does not guarantee a majority.

Nor does one election permanently dismantle the movement that deployed it. Republican leaders retain institutions, donors and an experienced propaganda network. A future presidential campaign led by someone such as JD Vance could again try to assemble power from the resentments Trump exploited.

But the 2026 results deny MAGA one of its most useful claims: that its cultural cruelty represents an irresistible popular will. In race after race, voters handed authority to the people its campaigns told them to fear. The propaganda named the targets. The electorate gave them power.

item.title: Trump’s strategy to save his own skin: Fight like a criminal
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s plan for surviving a Democratic Congress is to use presidential power to obstruct its scrutiny. According to The New York Times , his White House is preparing to cast some legislative oversight as potentially criminal, expand executive-privilege claims and coordinate with the Justice Department and congressional Republicans to resist subpoenas and records requests. The strategy is not evidence that Trump has committed a crime. It is evidence that his administration intends to trea
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s plan for surviving a Democratic Congress is to use presidential power to obstruct its scrutiny. According to The New York Times, his White House is preparing to cast some legislative oversight as potentially criminal, expand executive-privilege claims and coordinate with the Justice Department and congressional Republicans to resist subpoenas and records requests. The strategy is not evidence that Trump has committed a crime. It is evidence that his administration intends to treat constitutionally assigned oversight as an attack to be defeated rather than a check to be obeyed.

The immediate stakes extend beyond Trump’s personal exposure. The anticipated inquiries could examine administration decisions, senior officials and wealthy private actors, including financial supporters who reportedly enriched Trump’s family during the previous two years or helped finance favored construction projects. By preparing to block access to that information, the White House is defending an entire network of power from public accounting.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Turning oversight into an offense

During Trump’s first term, resistance depended heavily on delay. The administration stonewalled congressional investigations and tried to run out the clock. The Times reports that the second-term plan is more aggressive: threaten to treat at least some oversight activity as a possible crime and wage what officials expect to be a two-year campaign against a Democratic Congress.

That escalation matters. A subpoena is not a criminal conspiracy simply because it is politically damaging. Congressional oversight is one of the legislature’s basic tools for examining executive conduct, spending and conflicts of interest. Recasting that authority as illegitimate—or potentially prosecutable—reverses the relationship between investigator and investigated. The officials controlling federal law enforcement would be positioned to intimidate the lawmakers charged with examining them.

White House spokesman Lauren Bis supplied the administration’s public framing in advance, telling the Times that Democrats pursuing “sham investigations and radical left policies” would be “choosing to work against the American people.” The wording performs a familiar substitution: Trump’s institutional interests become the public interest, while scrutiny of his administration becomes hostility toward the country. It offers no distinction between a genuinely abusive inquiry and any investigation the White House finds threatening.

Stephen Miller’s machinery of resistance

Trump’s incoming chief of staff, Stephen Miller, is expected to direct the defense. The Times describes Miller as an experienced Capitol Hill combatant, but this will not be a personal operation conducted from one West Wing office. The White House Counsel’s Office and the Justice Department have reportedly been preparing for a prolonged confrontation.

The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel has already produced one potentially powerful shield. According to the Times, it issued an opinion months earlier saying executive privilege could cover communications involving people outside government when those communications concern Trump and senior aides. If applied broadly, that position could place dealings with donors and other private power brokers behind an executive-branch barrier ordinarily associated with official presidential deliberations.

Republican congressional staff are also expected to assist the department in answering Democratic subpoenas, document demands and allegations. Rachel Jag, formerly an aide to Republican Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, is overseeing a large staff as the department seeks more experienced lawyers for the expected workload.

That hiring effort is colliding with another consequence of Trump’s rule: the Times reports that the Justice Department has suffered extensive departures following his politicization of the institution. The administration is trying to build a legal fortress with an agency it has depleted, using remaining public capacity to protect the executive branch from another elected branch.

The scrutiny Republicans declined to provide

Democrats preparing to assume the congressional majority in January had already sent letters to scores of prospective investigative targets, the Times reported. The subjects ranged from cuts to scientific research to donors supporting Trump’s White House ballroom. Democratic lawmakers reportedly showed no intention of retreating from what the administration expected to be a relentless oversight schedule.

That agenda follows a Republican Congress that declined to police the Trump administration with comparable force. Its abdication did more than spare the president embarrassment. It allowed executive decisions, financial relationships and the conduct of powerful officials to escape the sustained scrutiny that Congress is institutionally equipped to provide.

The coming conflict is therefore not merely a partisan quarrel between Democrats seeking documents and Republicans withholding them. One side is preparing to exercise congressional investigative authority. The executive branch, aided by the department that controls federal prosecution, is preparing to portray that exercise as abuse and possibly criminal conduct.

The headline’s image of Trump fighting “like a criminal” overstates what the reporting establishes: the account does not prove criminality. The documented maneuver is grave enough without that shortcut. A president worried about investigations is mobilizing lawyers, prosecutors, privilege claims and partisan allies to prevent Congress from learning how his administration operates and whom it benefits. The unresolved question is whether those institutions will serve their public functions—or the personal defenses of the man who controls them.

item.title: Chaos predicted as spiraling Trump sets the tone for lame-duck GOP
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s promised congressional “rubber stamp” did not survive the election. As reported by AlterNet, citing Slate senior editor Jim Newell, Democrats are set to control the Senate, Republicans will enter the next House as a smaller and more ideologically concentrated minority, and the president now faces a closing window in which to entrench his personnel and policy choices. The likely result is not merely disorder. It is a hurried exercise of power before voters’ decision takes effect. T
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s promised congressional “rubber stamp” did not survive the election. As reported by AlterNet, citing Slate senior editor Jim Newell, Democrats are set to control the Senate, Republicans will enter the next House as a smaller and more ideologically concentrated minority, and the president now faces a closing window in which to entrench his personnel and policy choices. The likely result is not merely disorder. It is a hurried exercise of power before voters’ decision takes effect.

Trump had spent six months predicting that Republicans would strengthen their position in Congress and shield the remaining two years of his second term from Democratic investigations. Instead, the GOP is preparing to relinquish what Newell described as “metric tons of political power” in January. That makes the lame-duck session consequential: an outgoing congressional majority still possesses the machinery to confirm judges, negotiate spending and attempt legislation whose effects will outlast its mandate.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A shrinking party elevates Jim Jordan

House Republicans selected Rep. Jim Jordan as their incoming leader, according to Slate. The promotion does not suggest that the election chastened the party into moderation. It indicates that defeat removed many of the Republicans who had electoral reasons to acknowledge swing voters, leaving the conference more thoroughly controlled by its combative right wing.

Newell argued that Jordan had not transformed himself from a factional provocateur into a broadly acceptable leader. Rather, Jordan’s faction had become what remained. That distinction matters. The voters reportedly reduced Republican power, but the surviving Republican caucus answered by elevating a politician identified with its most confrontational tendencies.

Institutional weakness and ideological moderation are not the same thing. A smaller House conference can have less power over legislation while becoming more disciplined around grievance, obstruction and spectacle. Jordan’s elevation points toward a minority leadership built to intensify conflict, not reconsider the choices that produced defeat.

The judiciary is the durable prize

The most achievable item on the lame-duck agenda is also the one with the longest reach. Republicans intend to fill roughly two dozen federal judicial vacancies before Democrats assume control of the Senate confirmation process, Newell reported. He expects judicial confirmations to consume most of the Senate’s floor time and force the Judiciary Committee to work quickly.

That is where the story’s loose talk of “chaos” can obscure the more important development. Trump may issue erratic late-night demands, and his administration may accelerate personnel changes before Democrats gain confirmation power. But Republicans also have a coherent institutional objective: place as many Trump nominees as possible on the federal bench while they still command the Senate.

Judges do not leave office when a congressional majority expires. Rapid confirmations would convert a temporary remainder of Republican power into durable control over parts of the judiciary. The electoral rebuke limits the party’s future authority; it does not erase the authority Republicans retain until the new Congress begins.

Trump’s Pentagon demand collides with Senate arithmetic

Trump is also directing congressional Republicans to provide the Pentagon with an additional $350 billion, above annual military funding that already exceeds $1 trillion, according to Newell. Enacting that demand would require Republicans to navigate a party-line reconciliation measure with little room for dissent.

That room is about to narrow. Newell reported that the Republican Senate majority would fall to 52 seats in December, when Sherrod Brown replaces Ohio Sen. Jon Husted following a special election. A last-minute reconciliation push could also destroy a broader government-funding agreement Republicans have negotiated with Democrats.

The choice exposes competing Republican priorities. Congress can preserve the funding deal, spend its limited floor time confirming judges or attempt to satisfy Trump’s enormous Pentagon request. It may not be able to do all three. Trump can issue orders to Republican lawmakers, but deadlines, vote counts and the approaching transfer of power remain less pliable than the congressional obedience he expected voters to preserve.

Personnel turmoil would serve a political purpose

Newell warned readers to expect a possible surprise before Democrats take control of Senate confirmations, including Cabinet departures or removals. He raised the prospect that Trump could replace officials while Republicans still possess the votes to confirm successors, though the report did not establish that any particular dismissal was imminent.

That possibility is more than presidential volatility. Changing Cabinet personnel before January would exploit the same closing window as the judicial push: use the defeated majority’s remaining authority before Democratic senators can block or scrutinize replacements. The spectacle may look improvised even when its consequences are concrete.

Republicans have spent Trump’s second term allowing the White House to set their agenda, Newell reported. Now that the president’s expected mandate has failed to materialize, the party has not produced an independent direction. Its surviving House members have promoted Jordan, its senators are racing the calendar on judges, and its legislative agenda remains vulnerable to Trump’s demands.

“Buckle up,” Newell concluded. The warning is apt, but the danger in the lame-duck period is not that nobody is in control. Trump retains the presidency, Republican senators retain their votes, and congressional leaders retain authority until the transfer occurs. The disorder lies in how those officials may use power after voters have already decided to take much of it away.

item.title: 'Buckle up': Experts warn Trump’s 'absurd' economy 'will end in tears'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s economic program is not the debt-erasing machine he advertised during the 2024 campaign. It is, in Andrew Neil’s account, an experiment in pushing monetary growth and federal borrowing at the wrong end of the economic cycle—leaving the Federal Reserve with fewer options if inflation persists or the artificial-intelligence boom collapses. Neil’s warning on The Andrew Neil Report was blunt: maintaining policies this loose under current conditions “will end in tears.” The arithmetic
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s economic program is not the debt-erasing machine he advertised during the 2024 campaign. It is, in Andrew Neil’s account, an experiment in pushing monetary growth and federal borrowing at the wrong end of the economic cycle—leaving the Federal Reserve with fewer options if inflation persists or the artificial-intelligence boom collapses. Neil’s warning on The Andrew Neil Report was blunt: maintaining policies this loose under current conditions “will end in tears.”

The arithmetic behind the warning

Trump promised to eliminate the national debt within one term without cutting Social Security or Medicare. His proposed escape route was extraordinary economic growth, tariffs and cryptocurrency—a collection of ambitions, not an explanation of how federal revenue would overtake spending and retire the accumulated debt.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Neil pointed instead to two indicators moving in the opposite direction. He said the American broad-money supply—the pool of liquid financial instruments held across money-holding sectors—was growing by 7 percent. He also placed the federal deficit at no less than 6.5 percent of gross domestic product and said it was probably heading toward 7 percent.

“In the late stages of this economic cycle monetary policy and fiscal policy are both running hot, hot, hot,” Neil told Gerard Baker, a Times columnist and Wall Street Journal editor at large. Governments and central banks ordinarily deploy that combination in response to recession, he argued, not while the cycle is already mature.

That distinction matters because Trump’s political salesmanship treats growth as an inexhaustible substitute for choices. It allows him to promise debt elimination, protect politically popular benefits and avoid identifying who would pay. The numbers Neil cited describe a government still borrowing heavily, not one approaching the wholesale retirement of its debt.

Divided government is not fiscal discipline

Neil also rejected the convenient assumption that a divided government would automatically constrain spending. His expectation was that budget negotiations would become an exchange of expensive concessions: more defense money traded for more health spending, or border-wall funding paired with additional welfare spending. Each side would secure its priority, and the deficit would grow.

That is not gridlock. It is an institutional incentive to finance agreement with borrowed money. The elected officials writing and approving budgets would remain responsible for those decisions; “horse trading” does not turn appropriations into an accident.

The political misdirection is already embedded in Trump’s promise. By claiming that tariffs, crypto and exceptional growth can erase the debt without benefit cuts, he removes Congress and the White House from the center of the story. Debt becomes a technical problem that prosperity will somehow solve, rather than the cumulative product of taxing and spending decisions made by people with power.

An AI reversal could expose the trap

Neil’s “nightmare scenario” is a collapse in the AI boom. In that event, he said, the Federal Reserve would have limited room to rescue the economy because interest rates and inflation were already high while the fiscal position was “completely out of control.” The danger he identified is stagflation: weak economic performance combined with persistent inflation.

That remains a forecast, not a reported outcome. AlterNet’s headline also stretches the evidence by advertising “experts” when its specific economic case rests overwhelmingly on Neil’s analysis. Baker supplied the political warning, telling listeners to “fasten your seatbelts,” but the figures and cycle argument came from Neil.

The underlying critique does not need embellishment. Trump promised the public that it could have debt elimination, untouched major benefits and spectacular growth without a credible account of the tradeoffs. Neil’s warning is that those tradeoffs have not disappeared. If the boom breaks, the bill will arrive when both fiscal policy and the Federal Reserve are less able to absorb it—and the people who made the promises will have every incentive to blame the crash rather than the choices that left the government exposed.
